MEDI2004 · Week 7 · Lecture 14

Small Molecules vs Biological Drugs

Two drug worlds sit side by side: the tiny, tablet-friendly chemicals that fill most prescriptions, and the huge, cell-grown proteins that swallow most of the budget. This guide decodes what makes a biologic different — and why size and structure dictate every one of its pharmacokinetic quirks.

§0Orientation · the landscape

Two worlds of drugs

Most prescriptions are small molecules; most of the money is biologics.

Before we can contrast small molecules with biologics, meet them in the wild. A small-molecule drug is a chemically synthesised, low-molecular-weight compound — aspirin is the textbook example at roughly 21 atoms and 180 daltons. A biological drug — also called a biopharmaceutical or biologic — is a large active substance produced by, or extracted from, a living organism, and it is usually given as an injection or infusion rather than a tablet. The whole lecture hangs on two learning objectives: distinguish small molecules from biologics, and understand why biologics have different pharmacokinetics.

🤔 Predict · before you read on

Australia's ten most-prescribed drugs and its ten most-expensive drugs barely overlap. Which class dominates each list?

By prescription count the top ten are almost all small molecules — statins (rosuvastatin, atorvastatin), proton-pump inhibitors (pantoprazole, esomeprazole), perindopril, escitalopram, metformin, sertraline, and the antibiotics amoxicillin and cefalexin. By cost to government the list flips to biologics and complex agents — pembrolizumab, nivolumab, ustekinumab, aflibercept, dupilumab, denosumab. The lesson: biologics are few by volume but enormous by spend.

Two league tables, two different worlds

Ranking Australia's PBS/RPBS drugs by prescription count (2023–24) gives a top ten that is essentially the small-molecule hall of fame: rosuvastatin (17.0 million scripts), atorvastatin, pantoprazole, esomeprazole, perindopril, escitalopram, metformin, sertraline, amoxicillin and cefalexin. Every one is a cheap, orally-active, mass-produced chemical. Re-rank the same system by cost to government and the leaderboard changes completely: pembrolizumab (~$580 million), the cystic-fibrosis combination elexacaftor–tezacaftor–ivacaftor, nivolumab, ustekinumab, aflibercept, dupilumab and denosumab climb to the top. Several of these are monoclonal antibodies dosed in tiny numbers of patients at very high unit price.

Reasoning · why the two lists barely overlap

The count list rewards chronic, common, cheap conditions treated by everyone (high cholesterol, reflux, hypertension, depression, infection) — small molecules that cost cents per dose. The cost list rewards expensive, targeted therapies for cancer and severe immune disease — biologics that can cost tens of thousands of dollars per patient-year. Because a biologic must be grown in living cells, purified and cold-chained, its unit cost is orders of magnitude higher, so even a handful of patients can top the spending chart.

Clinical / real-world

This split drives real prescribing and reimbursement policy. Small molecules are the workhorses of primary care — a GP can start a statin or a PPI on the spot. Biologics are gatekept: they need specialist initiation, strict PBS authority criteria, and often a failed trial of cheaper therapy first, precisely because each script commits the health system to a very large bill.

R Recall — the landscape
  • Small-molecule drug — chemically synthesised, low molecular weight (aspirin ≈180 Da), usually oral.
  • Biologic / biopharmaceutical — large active substance made by a living organism, usually injected.
  • Top by prescription count — almost all small molecules (statins, PPIs, metformin, antibiotics).
  • Top by cost — biologics dominate (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, dupilumab, denosumab).
  • Two learning objectives — distinguish the two classes, and explain WHY biologics have different PK.
§1Definitions · the family tree

What are biological drugs?

Proteins, antibodies and oligonucleotides — made by life, used as medicine.

A biological (biopharmaceutical, biologic) contains an active substance derived from or extracted from a biological system — a living organism. That single sentence separates it from a small molecule, which is built atom-by-atom in a chemistry lab. The biologic family has three main members: proteins, antibodies (a special kind of protein) and oligonucleotides (short nucleic-acid strands). The rest of the lecture is really a tour of these three, plus the pharmacokinetic consequences of being big.

First-generation vs second-generation

  • First-generation biologics — the natural human sequence produced recombinantly, e.g. native human insulin. The aim is simply to reproduce the molecule the body already makes.
  • Second-generation biologics — the protein is deliberately engineered (its gene sequence changed, or chemically modified) to improve properties such as half-life, solubility or immunogenicity. We meet these in §2.2.

What biologics are used for

  • Therapeutic monoclonal antibodies — targeted proteins that bind one antigen (the –mab drugs of §3).
  • Recombinant hormones — replacing a missing protein hormone, e.g. insulin or growth hormone (§2).
  • Controlling gene expression — oligonucleotide and gene therapies that switch a gene on or off (§6).
Reasoning · why "made by life" changes everything

Because the active substance is produced inside living cells, it is a large, folded, often glycosylated molecule — not a small rigid chemical. That biological origin is the root cause of every downstream difference we will meet: the size (§4), the parenteral route, the immunogenicity, the manufacturing variability (§5). Hold onto the phrase "derived from a living organism" — it is the seed of the whole contrast.

Memory hook · "PAO"

Biologics = Proteins, Antibodies, Oligonucleotides.

Three letters, three sections ahead: Protein hormones (§2), Antibodies (§3), Oligonucleotides & gene therapy (§6).

Clinical / real-world

The definition matters legally and practically. Regulators (TGA, FDA) treat biologics under a separate framework from chemically-synthesised drugs, with extra rules on manufacturing consistency, cold-chain storage and post-market surveillance — all because the product is grown, not synthesised. It also explains why a "biosimilar" (§5) is a regulatory category that simply does not exist for a small-molecule generic.

R Recall — defining biologics
  • Biologic definition — active substance derived from / extracted from a living organism.
  • Three members — proteins, antibodies, oligonucleotides.
  • First-generation — the natural recombinant sequence (e.g. native insulin).
  • Second-generation — deliberately engineered to improve properties.
  • Applications — therapeutic mAbs, recombinant hormones, controlling gene expression.
§2Manufacture · recombinant proteins

Making proteins as drugs

From scarce tissue extracts to genes grown in cell factories.

Protein-hormone drugs are not a new idea — insulin and growth hormone have been used for decades. What changed was how we make them. For much of the twentieth century the only option was purified extracts from animal or cadaver tissue: scarce, batch-variable, and prone to triggering immune reactions or transmitting disease. Recombinant DNA technology replaced all that — we now grow the human protein to order.

Label Key — the recombinant workflow
Human cell / Insulin gene
The source of the human DNA sequence that codes the desired protein. Using the human gene means the product is the true human protein, not an animal analogue — so it works and is far less immunogenic.
Recombinant plasmid
A bacterial circular DNA vector into which the human gene is spliced. The plasmid is the delivery vehicle that carries the human instruction into a bacterium.
Transgenic bacteria
Bacteria that have taken up the recombinant plasmid and now read the human gene as if it were their own — turning each cell into a tiny protein factory.
Grow in culture
Mass-amplification step: billions of identical transgenic cells are grown, each churning out the protein — this is what makes recombinant supply effectively unlimited.
Extract insulin
The harvest & purify step — the protein is separated from the cells and contaminants to pharmaceutical purity, ready to inject.

As Plate 2.1 shows, the process reduces to two core steps: 1 — insert the human gene into a suitable expression system, and 2 — harvest and purify the recombinant protein. Everything else in the diagram (plasmid, transformation, culture) is machinery serving those two ideas.

Reasoning · why recombinant beats extraction

Extracted insulin came from pig or cattle pancreas: supply was limited by animal availability, the sequence differed slightly from human (so it could provoke antibodies), and purification was imperfect. Recombinant production gives the exact human sequence, in unlimited, consistent quantity, free of animal pathogens. Form follows source: identical genetic template → identical protein every batch, in principle.

Clinical / real-world

Before recombinant human growth hormone, hGH was extracted from cadaver pituitaries — and some recipients later developed Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease from prion-contaminated batches. Recombinant manufacture (a defined gene grown in a controlled cell line) eliminated that transmission risk. It is a concrete illustration of why "grown from a known gene" is safer than "extracted from tissue".

§2.1Choosing an expression system

Step 1 above hides a real decision: which living organism grows the protein? A protein expression system is simply the type of living organism used to produce the desired protein — and the choice is not trivial.

Label Key — the three host systems
Bacteria
Cheapest and fastest host (e.g. E. coli). Great for simple proteins, but bacteria cannot glycosylate or fold the most complex human proteins — so quality is limited for anything intricate.
Yeast
A middle ground: eukaryotic, so it can do some folding and glycosylation, still relatively cheap and scalable — useful when bacteria are too crude but mammalian cells are overkill.
Mammalian cells
Most human-like output: correct folding and human-type glycosylation, essential for antibodies and complex proteins — but slow, expensive and demanding to culture.
"Each system varies…"
The key caption: hosts differ in protein quality, cost, expression amount and speed — the four trade-offs that decide the choice.

Plate 2.2 lines up the three usual hosts — bacteria, yeast and mammalian cells — and the take-home is the grey caption: each varies in protein quality, cost, expression amount and speed. There is no universally best system; you match the host to the molecule.

Reasoning · why not always use cheap bacteria?

Because complex human proteins need post-translational modification — especially glycosylation (adding sugar chains) and correct disulphide-bond folding — and bacteria simply lack that machinery. A monoclonal antibody made in E. coli would be misfolded and non-functional. So you pay for mammalian cells when the molecule demands human-style processing, and save with bacteria when it doesn't (as for insulin, a small protein).

Clinical / real-world

The host system is baked into the product's identity and cannot be casually swapped — change the cell line and you change the glycosylation pattern, which can alter efficacy and immunogenicity. This is a major reason a biosimilar (§5) can never be proven identical: a different manufacturer, using a different cell line and process, cannot recreate the exact glycan fingerprint of the originator.

§2.2Engineered proteins & PEGylation

Second-generation biologics go further than copying nature: they alter the protein before expression (for example by changing the gene sequence) to modify its pharmacokinetics or to build novel fusion proteins. A classic post-production modification is PEGylation — attaching chains of polyethylene glycol (PEG) to the protein.

Label Key — advantages of PEGylation
PEG chains
Inert, flexible polyethylene-glycol strands chemically bonded to the protein — they form a hydrated shell around it without touching its active site.
Size increase → ↓ kidney filtration
The bulky PEG shell raises the effective molecular size above the renal filtration threshold, so the drug is cleared far more slowly — the main driver of a longer half-life.
Reduced accessibility for proteases & antibodies
PEG physically shields the protein surface, hiding it from degrading enzymes and from the immune system — so it survives longer and is less immunogenic ("humanising").
Hydrophilicity of PEG
PEG is water-loving, so it increases the drug's solubility — easier to formulate and inject at useful concentrations.

Plate 2.3 packs three benefits into one picture. Trace them: the size increase reduces kidney filtration (top-to-bottom arrow) → longer half-life; the shielding gives reduced accessibility for proteases and antibodies → less breakdown and reduced immunogenicity; and PEG's hydrophilicity increases drug solubility. The lecture explicitly lists PEGylation's advantages as reducing immunogenicity (humanising proteins) alongside the PK improvements.

Reasoning · why bigger = longer-lasting

The kidney's glomerulus filters small molecules freely but retains large ones — the practical cut-off is around 30–50 kDa. A small therapeutic protein below that size is filtered out in the urine within minutes to hours. Bolt on PEG and the effective size jumps above the threshold, so renal clearance drops and the drug persists. It's the same principle as §4: size controls clearance, and PEGylation is a deliberate way to exploit it.

Clinical / real-world

PEGylation turns an impractical daily injection into a weekly or fortnightly one. Pegfilgrastim (PEGylated G-CSF) is given once per chemotherapy cycle instead of daily filgrastim; PEG-interferon allowed weekly rather than thrice-weekly dosing in hepatitis C. Fewer injections means better adherence and quality of life — a direct patient benefit that flows straight from the half-life mechanism.

R Recall — making proteins
  • Old method — purified tissue extracts (scarce, variable, immunogenic).
  • Recombinant steps — 1 insert gene into expression system, 2 harvest and purify protein.
  • Expression system — the living organism (bacteria / yeast / mammalian) used to grow the protein.
  • System trade-offs — protein quality, cost, expression amount, speed.
  • PEGylation gives — longer half-life (↓ renal filtration), less immunogenicity/proteolysis, more solubility.
§3The –mab drugs

Monoclonal antibodies

One clone, one epitope — the immune system turned into a precision drug.

Antibodies are large proteins produced by activated B cells (plasma cells), and they are central to the immune system. Each antibody binds a specific antigen, and that binding produces effects such as neutralization, agglutination and precipitation. A monoclonal antibody (mAb) is made by identical immune cells so that every molecule binds the same epitope — a single, pure specificity you can use as a drug. The give-away in the name: all monoclonal antibody drugs end in –mab (infliximab, omalizumab, adalimumab).

Label Key — the hybridoma workflow
Mouse challenged with antigen
Priming step: the animal mounts an immune response, generating B cells that make antibody against the chosen target.
Spleen cells
The harvested antibody-producing B cells — they have the specificity you want, but die quickly in culture.
Myeloma cells
Immortal cancer cells that divide indefinitely but make no useful antibody — they supply longevity.
Fusion → hybridomas
Merging spleen + myeloma yields hybridomas: immortal AND antibody-producing — the best of both parents.
Culture in HAT medium / select
A selective medium that only fused hybridomas survive, weeding out unfused cells so you keep the positive antibody-makers.
Harvest monoclonal antibodies
The purified single-specificity antibody — every molecule identical, binding one epitope: the drug.

Plate 3.1 walks the classic hybridoma route. Follow the arrows: a mouse is challenged with antigen; its spleen cells (which make the antibody but are mortal) are fused with myeloma cells (which are immortal but useless on their own) to form hybridomas; these are grown in HAT medium that selects only the fused, positive cells; and finally the monoclonal antibody is harvested. The trick of the method is combining two half-solutions into one whole.

Reasoning · why fuse two cell types?

Neither parent alone can do the job. B cells have the specificity (they make exactly the antibody you want) but they senesce and die in culture. Myeloma cells have immortality (endless division) but no useful specificity. Fusion combines the specificity of one with the immortality of the other, so a single clone can be grown forever, each cell secreting the identical antibody — that is what makes the product truly "monoclonal".

Memory hook · read the suffix

If it ends in –mab, it's a Monoclonal AntiBody.

Infliximab, omalizumab, adalimumab, pembrolizumab, nivolumab — every one is a large protein drug given parenterally, so the naming instantly tells you the pharmacokinetic class.

Clinical / real-world

Original mouse-derived mAbs provoked human anti-mouse antibody responses (loss of effect, allergic reactions) — precisely because the protein was foreign. Later engineering humanised or fully-humanised the sequence (reflected in the naming stems), reducing immunogenicity. It is the same theme as PEGylation (§2.2): the more human-like the protein, the less the immune system attacks the drug.

R Recall — monoclonal antibodies
  • Antibody source — large proteins made by activated B cells (plasma cells).
  • Binding effects — neutralization, agglutination, precipitation.
  • "Monoclonal" means — made by identical cells, all binding the same epitope.
  • Hybridoma trick — fuse specific (mortal) B cells with immortal myeloma cells.
  • Naming rule — all monoclonal antibody drugs end in –mab.
§4The core contrast · why PK differs

Size, structure & pharmacokinetics

Biologics are literally big — and every PK quirk falls out of that one fact.

This is the heart of the lecture, and the second learning objective: why do biologics have different pharmacokinetics? The answer is a single word — size — plus its companion, structural complexity. Once you accept that a biologic is thousands of times larger and more intricate than a small molecule, every difference in route, half-life, immunogenicity and interaction potential follows logically.

Label Key — the size gap
Aspirin — 21 atoms / 180 daltons
The small-molecule benchmark: tiny, rigid, fully defined. Small enough to diffuse across membranes and be filtered/metabolised readily.
Typical monoclonal Ab — 20,000 atoms / 150,000 daltons
Roughly ~1000× the mass of aspirin. Too big to cross membranes, too big for rapid renal filtration — the physical basis of its long half-life and parenteral route.

Plate 4.1 makes the gap visceral: aspirin is 21 atoms / 180 daltons; a typical monoclonal antibody is 20,000 atoms / 150,000 daltons — about a thousand-fold heavier. That is not a minor difference of degree; it is a different physical regime.

Label Key — the analogy grid
Aspirin ≈ 21 atoms → Bike (~20 lb)
Simple enough that anyone can build and copy it exactly — the small-molecule end.
hGH ≈ 3000 atoms → Car (~3000 lb)
A large-molecule drug: far more parts, harder to make, but still a defined manufactured object.
IgG antibody ≈ 25,000 atoms → Business jet (~30,000 lb)
A large biologic: thousands of precisely-arranged parts. So intricate that no two builds are truly identical — foreshadowing §5.

Plate 4.2 ranks three tiers by both size and complexity. In the size row: aspirin (~21 atoms), human growth hormone (~3000 atoms), and an IgG antibody (~25,000 atoms). The complexity row translates that into everyday objects — a bike (~20 lb), a car (~3000 lb), and a business jet (~30,000 lb, without fuel). The analogy previews §5: you can mass-produce identical bikes, but no two hand-built jets are ever exactly the same.

🤔 Predict · before the tables

Given that a biologic is a huge, water-loving protein, which will be true of it: can it cross cell membranes? swallow it as a tablet? does it have many CYP drug interactions?

All three answers favour "no". A biologic cannot easily cross cell membranes (too big, too polar), has very low oral bioavailability (digested by gut proteases and acid, so it must be injected), and has few classic drug interactions (it isn't a CYP450 substrate — it's broken down to amino acids by proteolysis). Its half-life is long, and it is more complex, not less, than a small molecule.

The exam-favourite question

The lecture poses: "Which of the following is correct regarding biological drugs?" — with tempting wrong options (they easily cross membranes / high oral bioavailability / more adverse effects / less complex). The single correct answer is that biologics have a (very) long half-life. Everything else is false: they cannot easily cross membranes, have low oral bioavailability, tend to have fewer adverse effects, and are more complex than small molecules.

Reasoning · one cause, many effects

Trace each PK property back to size/structure. Can't cross membranes → large and polar, so no passive diffusion → must be given parenterally, and acts on cell-surface or extracellular targets. Low oral bioavailability → a protein swallowed is digested like food by gastric acid and proteases. Long half-life → too big for rapid renal filtration, and antibodies are actively recycled (see below). Few drug interactions → not a CYP450 substrate, so no competition at metabolic enzymes. One physical fact — bigness — radiates into the whole PK profile.

§4.1The comparison tables (Rang & Dale)

Two reference tables from Rang & Dale's Pharmacology nail the contrast property-by-property.

Label Key — Table 5.2 rows
Size
Conventional <500 Da (10²); biopharmaceutical >5000 Da — oligonucleotides ~10³, small proteins 10³–10⁴, mAbs ~10⁵, genes >10⁶. The root difference.
Synthesis
Conventional = easy identical batches; biologics are unique (except small peptides / short oligonucleotides made chemically) — why biosimilars exist (§5).
Dose–effect
Conventional = predictable; biologics = complex mechanisms, high-affinity binding, slow on/off-rates, unusual D/R curves.
Pharmacokinetics
Conventional = often oral, variable absorption, phase 1&2 metabolism, renal/faecal excretion; biologics = parenteral, high bioavailability, long half-life, atypical distribution/removal.
Toxicology & adverse effects
Conventional = variable, possible drug interactions; biologics = immunogenicity, few drug interactions, generally fewer adverse effects.

Plate 4.3 (Table 5.2) is the master comparison. Read it as a set of consequences of size: conventional drugs are small (<500 Da), easy to batch-synthesise identically, predictable in dose–effect, often oral, and metabolised by classic phase 1/2 pathways; biopharmaceuticals are large (>5000 Da), essentially unique molecules, have complex high-affinity mechanisms with unusual dose–response curves, are given parenterally with long half-lives, and their main safety issue is immunogenicity rather than drug interactions.

Label Key — Table 5.3 columns
Route
Small molecules p.o. (by mouth); biologics i.m. (parenteral) — the membrane/digestion problem forces injection.
Dosing frequency
Small molecules daily; biologics weekly → monthly — a direct read-out of their long half-life.
Tmax / T½
Small molecules: T½ ~1.5–3 h. Biologics: etanercept 102 h, adalimumab 10–20 days, omalizumab 26 days.
Bioavailability
Wildly variable for oral drugs (simvastatin <5% vs indometacin >90%); biologics ~58–64% once injected (bypassing the gut).
V (volume of distribution)
Biologics have a small V (few litres) — they stay largely in plasma/extracellular fluid because they can't cross membranes into tissues.

Plate 4.4 (Table 5.3) puts numbers on it. The two conventional drugs — simvastatin and indometacin — are oral with half-lives of hours (1.5 h and 2–3 h). The three biologics — etanercept, adalimumab and omalizumab — are all intramuscular, dosed weekly to monthly, with half-lives of days to weeks (up to 26 days). Notice the small volumes of distribution: because biologics can't cross into tissues, they stay in the plasma/extracellular compartment.

Worked example · how much longer does an antibody last?

Compare simvastatin (T½ ≈ 1.5 h) with the monoclonal antibody omalizumab (T½ ≈ 26 days). How many times longer is the antibody's half-life, and what does that mean for dosing?

  1. Put both half-lives in the same units. Omalizumab: 26 days × 24 h/day = 624 h.
  2. Take the ratio: 624 h ÷ 1.5 h ≈ 416. The antibody's half-life is roughly 400× longer.
  3. Interpret via dosing. A drug is dosed roughly every one to a few half-lives to hold steady levels. Simvastatin (T½ 1.5 h, though dosed once daily using its pharmacodynamic effect) versus omalizumab, whose ~26-day half-life allows once-monthly injection.
  4. Trace the cause: the ~1000× size increase (Plate 4.1) blocks rapid renal filtration, and antibodies are additionally recycled (below) — together stretching hours into weeks.

Answer: ~400× longer half-life → hours-scale (daily) dosing for the small molecule vs weeks-scale (monthly) dosing for the antibody.

Why immunoglobulins outlast other plasma proteins

The lecture adds a key detail: antibodies (immunoglobulins) have a longer half-life than most plasma proteins. Specifically, IgG lasts ~21 days, whereas IgA and IgM last only ~5–6 days. IgG is the outlier.

Reasoning · the FcRn recycling pump

IgG's exceptional ~21-day survival comes from the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn). Cells constantly pinocytose plasma proteins; inside the acidified endosome, FcRn grabs IgG's Fc region and, instead of sending it to lysosomal destruction, ships it back to the cell surface and releases it at neutral pH — rescuing it into the circulation. IgA and IgM lack this rescue, so they are degraded on the normal timescale. This is why most therapeutic mAbs (IgG-based) inherit a multi-week half-life, and why engineers tune FcRn binding to lengthen it further.

Clinical / real-world

The long half-life is a double-edged sword. It permits convenient monthly dosing and durable effect — but if a patient develops a severe adverse reaction (e.g. infection risk from immunosuppression, or an infusion reaction), the drug cannot be quickly withdrawn: it lingers for weeks. There is no dialysing off a monoclonal antibody. Clinicians must weigh that irreversibility, especially before surgery or when infection appears.

R Recall — size & pharmacokinetics
  • Size gap — aspirin ~180 Da / 21 atoms vs mAb ~150,000 Da / 20,000 atoms (~1000×).
  • Conventional vs biologic size — <500 Da vs >5000 Da.
  • Biologic PK profile — parenteral, low oral bioavailability, can't cross membranes, long half-life.
  • The correct MCQ answer — biologics have a (very) long half-life.
  • IgG half-life — ~21 days (vs IgA/IgM ~5–6 days), via FcRn recycling.
  • Drug interactions — few, because biologics aren't CYP450 substrates.
§5Copies · generics vs biosimilars

Can they be reproduced?

A small molecule you can copy exactly; a biologic you can only make similar.

The complexity of §4 has a commercial and regulatory sting in its tail: can you copy the drug when the patent expires? For small molecules, yes — exactly. For biologics, no — only approximately. That distinction is the whole reason the word biosimilar exists.

Label Key — the reproducibility contrast
Small molecule "="
Two identical chemical structures joined by an equals sign: because a small molecule is small, fully definable and well-characterised, a copy is chemically identical — a true generic.
Large molecule "≠"
Two antibodies joined by a not-equal sign: biologics are too complex to characterise fully and depend on the manufacturing process, so a follow-on version is similar, not identical — a biosimilar.

Plate 5.1 states it with two symbols. On the left, can small-molecule medicines be reproduced? — Yes: they are relatively small, can be completely defined, are well-characterised, and entirely reproduced (the "=" sign). On the right, can large-molecule biologics be reproduced? — No: most biologics are complex molecules that are not as easily characterised, and come with unique challenges that must be managed throughout manufacturing (the "≠" sign).

Reasoning · why "similar" is the best you can do

A small molecule is a defined arrangement of a few dozen atoms — analyse it and you know it completely, so a second factory can make the same thing. A biologic is thousands of atoms folded into a precise 3-D shape with sugar chains added by living cells; its final structure depends on the process (cell line, culture conditions, purification). Change the process and you change the product subtly. Since no rival can copy the originator's exact process, the copy can only be shown to be highly similar — hence biosimilar, never "bio-identical".

Memory hook · = vs ≠

Small molecule = generic (=). Biologic = biosimilar (≠).

"Generic" claims identity; "biosimilar" only claims similarity. The symbol from Plate 5.1 is the exam answer in one glyph.

Clinical / real-world

Because a biosimilar isn't proven identical, regulators require its own clinical comparability studies before approval, and substitution at the pharmacy is handled more cautiously than for generics. Even so, biosimilars still slash cost — when the patent on an expensive originator (say adalimumab) expires, biosimilar competition can bring the price down substantially, expanding access to therapies that previously topped the spending charts of §0.

R Recall — reproducibility
  • Small molecules — can be reproduced exactly (fully defined, well-characterised) → generic.
  • Biologics — cannot be reproduced identically (too complex, process-dependent) → biosimilar.
  • Why not identical — structure depends on the living-cell manufacturing process.
  • Regulatory consequence — biosimilars need their own comparability trials.
§6Nucleic-acid drugs

Oligonucleotides & gene therapy

Drugging the gene, not the protein — the third branch of biologics.

The final member of the biologic family (the "O" of P-A-O) is the oligonucleotide — a short nucleic-acid strand used as a drug. These agents act one step upstream of proteins, at the level of the gene or its messenger RNA. Gene therapy is the umbrella idea: the addition of genetic material to cells to prevent, alleviate or cure disease.

What gene therapy could treat

  • Monogenic diseases — conditions caused by a single defective gene, such as cystic fibrosis and the haemoglobinopathies: fix or supply the one faulty gene.
  • Conditions with or without a genetic component — many malignant, neurodegenerative and infectious diseases, where added genetic material can modify the disease course.
Label Key — the antisense mechanism
DNA → Transcription → mRNA
The normal first step of gene expression: the gene is copied into messenger RNA, the template for the protein.
Antisense drug (oligonucleotide)
A short strand with a sequence complementary to the "sense" mRNA. It base-pairs with the mRNA and clamps onto it.
Translation ✗
With the antisense drug bound, the mRNA cannot be translated — the ribosome is blocked, so the protein is never made.
Proteins → DISEASE (blocked)
The disease-causing protein is not produced, interrupting the pathway that leads to disease — the therapeutic goal.

Plate 6.1 shows the mechanism on the central-dogma backbone. Normally DNA is transcribed to mRNA and translated to protein. An antisense oligonucleotide binds the complementary ("sense") mRNA sequence and blocks translation — the ribosome cannot read a double-stranded message, so the disease-causing protein is never made. It's a molecular off-switch placed at the mRNA step.

Reasoning · why target mRNA rather than the protein?

A small-molecule or antibody drug can only inhibit a protein after it exists — and only if it has a druggable pocket. Many disease proteins are "undruggable" (no good binding site) or act intracellularly where antibodies can't reach. Antisense sidesteps this by stopping the protein being made at all, and it is exquisitely selective because base-pairing rules mean it recognises one specific sequence. The trade-off: it must reach the inside of the target cell, which is the delivery challenge below.

Clinical / real-world · distribution & the CNS gap

After parenteral administration, oligonucleotides distribute widely throughout the body — with the exception of the CNS, because they don't cross the blood–brain barrier. Clinically this is decisive: to treat a neurological disease like spinal muscular atrophy, the antisense drug nusinersen must be injected intrathecally (into the CSF) rather than into a vein. The BBB that protects the brain also locks these drugs out of it.

§6.1Delivery systems — the real hurdle

Whatever the genetic payload, getting it inside the right cell is the bottleneck. As the lecture states plainly: gene delivery is the main hurdle to practical gene therapy. An ideal vector should be safe, efficient, selective, and produce long-lasting expression of the therapeutic gene. Delivery splits into viral vectors and non-viral vectors.

Label Key — adenoviral delivery, step by step
Modified DNA injected into vector
The therapeutic new gene is packaged between viral DNA inside the adenovirus shell — the virus becomes a courier, stripped of its ability to cause disease.
Vector binds to cell membrane
The virus's surface proteins dock onto receptors on the target cell — the selectivity step.
Vector packaged in vesicle
The cell engulfs the vector into an endocytic vesicle, drawing it inside.
Vesicle breaks down, releasing vector
The vesicle ruptures, freeing the vector into the cytoplasm so it can travel onward.
Vector injects new gene into nucleus
The vector delivers the therapeutic gene into the nucleus, where the cell's machinery can read it.
Cell makes protein using new gene
The endpoint: the cell expresses the therapeutic protein from the delivered gene — the cure in action.

Trace the arrows in Plate 6.2: the therapeutic gene is packaged into the adenovirus (modified DNA injected into vector); the vector binds the cell membrane; it is packaged in a vesicle; the vesicle breaks down releasing the vector; the vector injects the new gene into the nucleus; and finally the cell makes protein using the new gene. Six steps from the outside of a cell to a working therapeutic protein.

Reasoning · why hijack a virus?

Viruses are nature's perfect gene-delivery machines — evolution has already solved the problems of binding a cell, getting inside, escaping the vesicle and reaching the nucleus. A viral vector is a virus with its disease-causing genes removed and the therapeutic gene inserted, so it delivers the payload without replicating or causing infection. That is why they are efficient. The catch — and why "safe, efficient, selective, long-lasting" is an ideal not a given — is that the immune system may still react to the viral shell, and off-target uptake can hit the wrong cells.

Clinical / real-world

Vector immunogenicity is not academic. Pre-existing immunity to common adenoviruses can neutralise the vector or trigger dangerous inflammatory responses, and high viral doses have caused fatal immune reactions historically. This is exactly why an ideal vector must be safe and selective, and why non-viral vectors (e.g. lipid nanoparticles) are pursued as alternatives — they trade some efficiency for a gentler immune profile.

R Recall — oligonucleotides & gene therapy
  • Gene therapy — adding genetic material to cells to prevent, alleviate or cure disease.
  • Best targets — monogenic diseases (cystic fibrosis, haemoglobinopathies) + malignant/neurodegenerative/infectious.
  • Antisense oligonucleotide — binds complementary mRNA and blocks translation.
  • Oligonucleotide distribution — wide, but NOT into the CNS (blood–brain barrier).
  • Main hurdle — gene delivery; ideal vector = safe, efficient, selective, long-lasting.
  • Vector types — viral (e.g. adenovirus) and non-viral.
